title: JavaScript Types & Coercion Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on JavaScript's primitive and reference types, typeof quirks, equality, truthiness, coercion rules, null vs undefined and NaN. Built for night-before revision with the gotchas interviewers love.

chapters.title: Primitives vs Reference Types
points: 7 primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol; everything else is an object (arrays, functions, dates, maps)
Primitives are immutable and copied by value: let b = a gives an independent copy; s[0]='X' on a string does nothing in sloppy mode and throws a TypeError in strict mode (modules, classes)
Objects are stored by reference: let b = a points both names at one object, so b.x = 1 changes a.x too
Comparison: primitives compare by value ('a'==='a' is true); objects compare by identity ({}==={} is false, [1]===[1] is false)
Mistake: const only freezes the binding, not the object; const o={}; o.x=1 works. Copy with {...o} or structuredClone(o) (spread is shallow, nested objects still shared)

chapters.title: typeof Quirks
points: typeof returns a string: 'string','number','bigint','boolean','undefined','symbol','object','function'
typeof null === 'object' is a legacy bug; test null with x === null
typeof [] and typeof new Date() are both 'object'; use Array.isArray(x) for arrays
typeof function(){} is 'function' though functions are objects; typeof class A{} is also 'function'
typeof on an undeclared variable returns 'undefined' with no error, but a let/const in its temporal dead zone throws ReferenceError

chapters.title: == vs ===
points: === compares type and value with no conversion; == converts operands first (loose equality). Default to ===
null == undefined is true, and neither equals anything else under ==; so x == null checks both null and undefined in one test

Loose rules: number vs string converts the string to a number ('5'==5 true); boolean converts to number first (true==1, '1'==true); object vs primitive calls ToPrimitive on the object ([1]==1 true, [1,2]=='1,2' true)
Surprise table: '' == 0 true, '0' == false true, '' == '0' false, [] == false true, [] == ![] true, null == 0 false
Object.is(a,b) is like === but Object.is(NaN,NaN) is true and Object.is(0,-0) is false

chapters.title: Truthy, Falsy and Coercion Rules
points: Exactly 8 falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '' (empty string), null, undefined, NaN; everything else is truthy
Surprise truthy: '0', 'false', [], {}, function(){}, new Boolean(false), -1, Infinity
+ with any string operand concatenates (1+'2'='12', [1]+[2]='12'); - * / % always convert to number ('6'-'2'=4, '3'*'4'=12)
ToNumber: ''→0, ' 12 '→12, 'abc'→NaN, null→0, undefined→NaN, true→1, []→0, [5]→5, {}→NaN
|| returns the first truthy operand, && the first falsy, ?? only skips null/undefined: 0 || 5 is 5 but 0 ?? 5 is 0; use ?? for defaults when 0 or '' are valid

chapters.title: null, undefined and NaN
points: undefined = no value assigned: uninitialised variable, missing property, missing argument, function with no return; null = intentional empty value set by the programmer
Comparison: typeof undefined is 'undefined' but typeof null is 'object'; Number(undefined) is NaN but Number(null) is 0; JSON.stringify drops undefined properties but keeps null
NaN is type number, produced by failed maths (0/0, Number('abc'), parseInt('x'), Math.sqrt(-1)); it is the only value not equal to itself, so NaN === NaN is false
Check with Number.isNaN(x) (strict, true only for NaN), not global isNaN('abc') which coerces first and returns true; [NaN].includes(NaN) is true but indexOf(NaN) is -1
Mistake: any arithmetic with NaN or undefined spreads NaN (undefined+1 is NaN, null+1 is 1); guard with ?. and ??, e.g. user?.age ?? 0

chapters.title: Types and Coercion Cheat Sheet
points: Types: 7 primitives by value, objects by reference; === on objects tests identity
typeof traps: null→'object', array→'object', function→'function'; use === null and Array.isArray
Falsy list: false 0 -0 0n '' null undefined NaN; everything else truthy, including '0', [] and {}
Coercion: + concatenates if any string, other operators convert to number; == only for x == null, otherwise ===
Checks: Number.isNaN for NaN, Object.is for NaN and -0, ?? for defaults that keep 0 and ''
